name: Honey (topical)
lead: Topical honey refers to honey applied to the skin, either as a home remedy and mask ingredient or as a processed ingredient in skincare. Honey is hygroscopic, meaning it draws in moisture, which is the basis for its use as a humectant [4]. It also has a long folk use on burns and skin injuries [4].

In appearance skincare, honey is promoted for hydration, softening and a 'brightening' or clarifying effect. Clinical research on honey has focused mainly on wound care and mucosal conditions rather than on cosmetic skin outcomes.
Wikipedia reports that medical-grade honey products have been approved by the FDA for minor wounds and burns, while evidence for many other uses is low quality [4].
infobox: Not recommended for infants under one (botulism) [4]

paras: Honey appears in DIY face masks and in commercial moisturisers, cleansers and masks, usually for hydration and softening. Traditional-brightener claims exist in beauty literature, but none of the sources reviewed provide controlled data on skin tone or pigmentation.

Honey has long been used as a topical antibacterial in traditional medicine, and its antibacterial effects were first reported in 1892; potency differs widely between honeys [4]. Wikipedia describes preliminary evidence that honey heals partial-thickness burns several days faster than other dressings and moderate evidence for faster healing of post-operative infections, with low-quality evidence for other wound uses [4]. Clinical reviews list honey among topical options for MRSA and chronic wounds [1][3].

Human trials of honey are largely in wound and oral settings. A randomized, blinded trial compared honey with a topical corticosteroid for recurrent minor aphthous ulcers [2]. A randomized assessor-masked trial of 16% manuka honey eye-drops studied meibomian gland dysfunction [5]. Registered trials include honey dressings versus EUSOL for wound infection, honey in deep neck abscess care, manuka honey after third-molar surgery, diabetic foot ulcers, perineal tear healing and honey versus alcohol as a skin disinfectant [6][7][8][9][10].
No controlled human study of honey for facial brightening, wrinkles or skin hydration was identified among the sources reviewed.

Honey is generally considered safe in typical food amounts, but infants under one year can develop botulism from honey containing Clostridium botulinum spores [4]. Wikipedia also notes possible interactions with allergies and that people with weakened immune systems may face infection risk [4]. Topical allergic reactions in sensitive individuals are possible, though the reviewed sources do not quantify them.

timeline.event: Antibacterial effects of honey first reported [4].

card.summary: A moisture-drawing pantry staple with real wound-care data but no controlled evidence yet for skin brightening.
card.note: Evidence is from wound care; cosmetic brightening is untested. Not for infants under one.

quick.overview:
Honey is used on skin as a mask or ingredient for hydration and a softer, brighter look. It has a long folk history on burns and wounds.

Trials exist for wounds, mouth ulcers and eye conditions, but none found address cosmetic brightening.
quick.mechanism: Honey is hygroscopic, so it attracts and holds water at the skin surface. Its antibacterial properties are attributed to compounds such as methylglyoxal and hydrogen peroxide, under preliminary study.
quick.risks: Generally well tolerated as a food. Infant botulism is the best-documented risk of honey, and allergy is possible in sensitive people.
